overview.text: An art museum is a permanent institution serving the public through visual art. It may collect works, research their histories, conserve them, and interpret and exhibit them; exhibitions can include borrowed works as well as objects in the museum’s own collection. These responsibilities make an art museum more than a display space: its collections and programs support learning, scholarship, and public engagement. By caring for artworks and presenting them in context, museums help people encounter ideas and artistic traditions across cultures and generations. Individual museums vary in scope, but their central role is to preserve and share art and the knowledge connected to it.

key_facts.text: ICOM’s museum definition describes museums as permanent, public-serving institutions that research, collect, conserve, interpret, and exhibit heritage, offering opportunities for education, enjoyment, reflection, and sharing knowledge.
Museum exhibitions may use works a museum owns, borrows, or creates for display; collections and exhibition materials can support research, exhibits, and public programs.
Collections stewardship includes caring for and preserving works, documenting them, and making collections and related information accessible responsibly.
Exhibitions, research, scholarship, publications, and educational activities are among the ways museums advance understanding and appreciation of cultural heritage.
The Met describes curatorial, conservation, and scientific research teams working together to study, exhibit, and care for its collection.
